title: Semiconductors and the Transistor
hook: The entire digital world rests on a tiny switch with no moving parts. The transistor — made from carefully tuned silicon — is the on/off building block behind every chip.
key_points: A semiconductor like silicon conducts electricity only sometimes — between conductor and insulator.
Adding trace impurities ('doping') precisely tunes how and when it conducts.
A transistor uses this to act as a switch: a small voltage controls a larger current.
Billions of transistors switching on and off encode the 1s and 0s of computing.
content_html: Materials usually fall into two camps: conductors like copper that let electricity flow, and insulators like glass that block it. Semiconductors — silicon above all — sit in between, conducting only under the right conditions. That in-between nature is exactly what makes them the most important materials of the modern age, because their conductivity can be precisely controlled. By adding minute traces of other elements, a process called doping, engineers dial in how a piece of silicon carries current.
extra_html: Combine doped regions cleverly and you get a transistor: a switch with no moving parts, in which a small voltage on one terminal turns the current between two others on or off. That simple controllable switch is the atom of computing. String billions of them together on a fingernail-sized chip and you can represent and manipulate information as patterns of on and off — the 1s and 0s of everything digital. Since the transistor's invention at Bell Labs in 1947, engineers have shrunk them relentlessly, packing ever more onto each chip, which is why phones now outclass the room-sized computers of decades past. Wikipedia covers how transistors are built and how they switch.

flashcards.prompt: What makes a semiconductor different from a normal conductor or insulator?
flashcards.back_html: It conducts electricity only sometimes — in between the two extremes — and that conductivity can be precisely controlled, which is what makes it so useful.

flashcards.prompt: What is the basic job of a transistor in a computer chip?

choices.text: Act as a switch where a small voltage turns a larger current on or off
Store electricity like a tiny battery

flashcards.explanation_html: A transistor lets one signal control another, switching between on and off — the physical embodiment of the 1s and 0s computers run on.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'doping' silicon with trace impurities so important?

choices.text: It tunes exactly how and when the silicon conducts, enabling transistors
It makes the silicon physically harder
It changes the silicon's color for labeling

flashcards.explanation_html: Adding tiny amounts of other elements controls the supply of mobile charges, which is how engineers build the switching behavior of a transistor.
